column2: Some philosophers have claimed that it [soothsaying] occurs only ahead of prophecy and then ceases, and that so it is with every prophecy that has occurred. The reason is that the existence of prophecy cannot be without a celestial configuration that requires it, and in the completeness of that configuration lies the completeness of the prophecy to which it points. The falling short of that configuration from completeness requires the existence of an incomplete nature of the kind that it requires, and this is the meaning of the soothsayer, as we have established. So before that complete configuration comes about, the incomplete configuration occurs and requires the existence of the soothsayer, whether one or several; and when that configuration is complete, the existence of the prophet in his perfection is complete, and the configurations that point to such a nature come to an end, so that nothing of it exists afterward. This rests on the assumption that part of a celestial configuration requires part of its effect, which is not conceded. Perhaps the configuration requires that effect only in its pure form, so that if some of its parts are lacking it requires nothing at all, and does not require the effect in a deficient form, as they have said. Further, these soothsayers, if they live in the time of prophecy, recognize the truthfulness of the prophet and the evidential force of his miracle, because they have some awareness of the matter of prophecy, as every human being has of the matter of sleep, and the intelligibility of that relation is present in the soothsayer more strongly than in the sleeper. Nothing holds them back from this and makes them fall into denial except the strength of their hope that it might be a prophecy for them, and so they fall into obstinacy, as happened to Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, who hoped to become a prophet; the same happened to Ibn Ṣayyād, to Musaylima and to others. But when faith prevails and those hopes are cut off, they believe with the best of belief, as happened to Ṭulayḥa al-Asadī and Suwād ibn Qārib, who left, in the Islamic conquests, traces that bear witness to the soundness of their faith.
Dream vision

As for the dream vision, its reality is the rational soul’s viewing, within its spiritual essence, of a flash of the forms of events. When the soul is spiritual, the forms of events exist in it in actuality, as is the case with all spiritual essences; and it becomes spiritual by divesting itself of corporeal matter and of the bodily faculties of perception. This may come to it as a flash by means of sleep, as we shall explain. By it the soul draws knowledge of the future matters it longs for, and returns with it to its faculties of perception. If that drawing is weak and not clear, it comes by imitation and likeness in the imagination, so that it may be extricated, and because of this imitation it needs interpretation. The drawing may be strong, so that imitation is dispensed with in it, and then it needs no interpretation, because it is free of likeness and imagination. The reason this flash occurs for the soul is that it is a spiritual essence in potentiality, brought to completion through the body and its faculties of perception until its essence becomes pure intellection and its existence is completed in actuality. It is then a spiritual essence that perceives without any of the bodily instruments, except that its kind among the spiritual beings is below the kind of the angels, the people of the highest horizon, who have not perfected their essences by any of the faculties of perception of the body or by anything else. This predisposition is present in the soul as long as it is in the body. Part of it is particular, like that of the saints, and part of it is general to humankind as a whole, and this is the matter of the dream vision.

As for what belongs to the prophets, it is a predisposition to strip itself of humanity into pure angelhood, which is the highest of the spiritual beings. This predisposition comes out in them repeatedly in the states of revelation, and when it turns to the bodily faculties of perception and whatever perception takes place in them occurs, it is plainly similar to the state of sleep, although the state of sleep is far below it. It is because of this similarity that the Lawgiver spoke of the dream vision as one part of forty-six parts of prophecy; in another version, forty-three, and in another, seventy. The number is not meant for its own sake in any of them; what is meant is multiplicity in the gradation of these ranks, as is shown by the mention of seventy in some of its chains of transmission, which among the Arabs is used to express abundance. What some have said regarding the version of forty-six, that revelation at its beginning came to him through dream vision for six months, which is half a year, while the whole duration of prophecy at Mecca and Medina was twenty-three years, so that half a year of it is one part of forty-six, is a statement far from verification, because that happened only to the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, and how do we know that this period applied to any other of the prophets? And that only gives the proportion of the time of the dream vision to the time of prophecy and does not give its reality in relation to the reality of prophecy.

And when this is clear to you from what we said at the outset, you will know that the meaning of this part is the proportion of the first predisposition, which includes all humankind, to the near predisposition that is particular to the class of the prophets and innate in them, God’s blessings be upon them, since the former is the remote predisposition: although it is general among humankind, it has with it many obstacles and impediments to its realization in actuality. One of the greatest of these obstacles is the outer senses. So God created human beings for the lifting of the veil of the senses in sleep, which is natural to them. When it is lifted, the soul is exposed to the knowledge of what it longs for in the world of truth, and at times it perceives from it a flash in which the object of its desire is attained. For that reason the Lawgiver counted it among the glad tidings (mubashshirāt). He said, “Nothing remains of prophecy except the glad tidings.” They said, “And what are the glad tidings, Messenger of God?” He said, “The good dream vision, which the righteous man sees or which is seen for him.” As for the reason the veil of the senses is lifted in sleep, it is as I shall describe to you. The rational soul perceives and acts only by means of the corporeal animal spirit, which is a subtle vapor whose center is in the left cavity of the heart, according to the books of anatomy by Galen and others. It spreads with the blood in the arteries and veins and gives sensation, movement and all the other bodily functions, and its subtlest part rises to the brain, where it tempers the brain’s coldness and the functions of the faculties in its ventricles are completed. So the rational soul perceives and understands only by means of this vaporous spirit,

and the soul is attached to it because of what the wisdom of generation required: that the subtle does not act upon the dense. Since this animal spirit is the subtlest of the bodily materials, it became the seat of the effects of the essence that is distinct from it in its corporeality, namely the rational soul, and the soul’s effects came to be realized in the body through it. We stated earlier that the soul’s perception is of two kinds: perception through the outer, which is the five senses, and perception through the inner, which is the faculties of the brain; and that all this perception turns it away from perceiving the spiritual essences above it, for which it is predisposed by innate disposition. Because the outer senses are corporeal, they are liable to drowsiness and weakening from the weariness and fatigue that overtake them, and to the overwhelming of the spirit by too much activity. So God created in them the desire for rest, so that perception may be pure in its perfect form. That comes about only through the animal spirit’s withdrawal from all the outer senses and its return to the inner sense. It is helped in this by the cold that comes over the body at night: the innate heat seeks the depths of the body and moves from its exterior to its interior, escorting its mount, which is the animal spirit, inward. For this reason human sleep is for the most part at night. So when the spirit withdraws from the outer senses and returns to the inner faculties, and the preoccupations and obstacles of sense are lightened for the soul, it returns to the forms in the memory, from which it forms, by combination,

and decomposition, forms of the imagination. Most of these are familiar, because they are drawn from perceptions recently attended to. Then the common sense, which is the collector of the outer senses, brings them down and perceives them in the modes of the five outer senses. Sometimes the soul turns a glance toward its spiritual essence, while contending with the inner faculties, and perceives with its spiritual perception, since it is innately disposed to it, and draws from the forms of the things that have then become attached to its essence. Then the imagination takes those perceived forms and represents them, either as they truly are or by imitation, in the familiar molds; and the imitation among these is what needs interpretation. The soul’s working by combination and decomposition on the forms in the memory, before it perceives from that flash what it perceives, is what constitutes jumbled dreams (aḍghāth aḥlām). In the Ṣaḥīḥ it is reported that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Dream visions are three: a dream vision from God, a dream vision from the angel, and a dream vision from the devil.” This classification agrees with what we have mentioned: the clear one is from God, the imitation that calls for interpretation is from the angel, and jumbled dreams are from the devil, because they are all falsehood and the devil is the wellspring of falsehood. This is the reality of the dream vision and of what causes it and accompanies it in sleep. These are properties of the human soul that are found in humankind generally; none of them is without them. Indeed every single human being has seen in his sleep, more than once, what then came to pass for him in his waking life, and it has become certain to him that the soul perceives the unseen in sleep without fail. And if that is possible in the world of sleep, it is not impossible in other states, since the perceiving essence is one and its properties are general to every state. And God is the guide to the truth, by His grace and bounty.

What happens to human beings of this kind is for the most part without intention and without power over it. The soul merely longs for that thing, and so it occurs, by that flash in sleep, because the soul is directed to it, and so it sees it. In the Kitāb al-Ghāya (“The Book of the Goal”) and other books of the people of spiritual exercises there is mention of names that are recited at sleep, from which a dream vision comes about concerning what one longs for; they call them ḥālūmiyya. Among them Maslama mentioned in the Kitāb al-Ghāya a ḥālūma that he called the ḥālūma of the Perfect Nature. It consists in saying, at the time of sleep, after the inner self is emptied and the orientation is sound, these non-Arabic words, which are “Tamāghis baʿd an yaswād wa-ghadās nūfanā ghādis,” and mentioning one’s need, whereupon one sees in sleep the disclosure of what one asked about. It is related that a man did this after some nights of spiritual exercise in his food and his invocation, and a figure appeared to him that said to him, “I am your Perfect Nature”; he asked it, and it told him about what he had longed for. This has happened to me myself with these names: wondrous visions, and by them I was made aware of matters concerning my own circumstances that I longed to know. That is not proof that the intention to have a dream vision brings it about; rather these ḥālūmas produce a predisposition in the soul for the occurrence of the dream vision, and when the predisposition is strong, it is nearer to the attainment of what it is predisposed for. A person may do as much preparation as he likes, and it is no proof that what he prepares for will be brought about; for the ability to prepare is not the ability over the thing itself. Know this, and ponder it in the similar cases you meet. And God is the Wise, the All-Aware.

Then we find in the human species individuals who report events before they occur, by a nature in them by which their class is distinguished from all other people. They do not resort to any craft for this, nor do they infer it from any sign of the stars or anything else; we find their perceptions in this only by virtue of their innate disposition on which they were created. Examples are the diviners (ʿarrāfūn) and those who look into transparent bodies such as mirrors and bowls of water, those who look into the hearts, livers and bones of animals, the people of augury (zajr) from birds and beasts of prey, and the people of ṭarq with pebbles and grains such as wheat and date stones. All these exist in the human world; no one can deny them or reject them. Likewise the insane, on whose tongues words of the unseen are cast, so that they report them; likewise the sleeper, and the dying man at the beginning of his death or his sleep, who speaks of the unseen; and likewise the practitioners of spiritual exercise among the Sufis, who have well-known perceptions of the unseen by way of saintly wonder (karāma).

We shall now speak about all these perceptions, beginning with soothsaying, and then take them up one by one to the last. Before that we shall put forward a preliminary, on how the human soul is predisposed to perceive the unseen in all the kinds we have mentioned. It is this: the soul is a spiritual essence existing in potentiality, passing to actuality through the body and its states, and this is a matter evident to everyone. Everything that is in potentiality has matter and form, and the form of this soul, by which its existence is completed, is perception and intellection themselves. So it exists first in potentiality, predisposed to perceive and to receive universal and particular forms; then its growth and its existence in actuality are completed through its association with the body, through what accustoms it, by the arrival upon it of its sensible perceptions, and through the universal meanings it abstracts from those perceptions. Thus it understands forms time after time until perception and intellection are attained by it in actuality, and its essence is completed; and the soul remains like prime matter, with forms succeeding one another upon it through perception, one after another. For this reason we find the child, at the beginning of his growth, unable to attain the perception that the soul has from its own essence, neither through sleep nor through unveiling nor through anything else; and that is because its form, which is its very essence, namely perception

and intellection, is not yet completed; indeed, the abstraction of universals is not yet completed for it. Then, when its essence is completed in actuality, it has, as long as it is with the body, two kinds of perception: perception by the instruments of the body, which the bodily faculties of perception convey to it, and perception by its own essence without an intermediary. From the latter it is veiled by its immersion in the body and the senses and their preoccupations, because the senses are always drawing it toward the outer by virtue of the bodily perception for which it was first created. Sometimes it plunges from the outer into the inner, and the veil of the body is lifted for a moment, either by a property that belongs to humans absolutely, such as sleep, or by a property found in some humans, such as soothsaying and ṭarq, or by spiritual exercise, as with the people of unveiling among the Sufis. It then turns to the essences above it that belong to the assembly (al-malaʾ), because of the connection in existence between its horizon and theirs, as we established before. Those essences are spiritual; they are pure perception and intellects in actuality, and in them are the forms of existing things and their realities, as has gone before. So something of those forms is disclosed in it, and it draws knowledge from them. Sometimes it passes those perceived forms to the imagination, which works them into the familiar molds; then it goes back to the senses with what it perceived, either bare or in its molds, and reports it.

This is the explanation of the soul’s predisposition for this perception of the unseen. Let us return to what we promised, the account of its kinds. As for those who look into transparent bodies, such as mirrors, bowls of water, and the hearts, livers and bones of animals, and the people of ṭarq with pebbles and date stones, all of them are of the type of soothsayers, except that they are lower in rank in it by the very origin of their creation, because the soothsayer does not need much labor to lift the veil of sense, whereas these labor at it by confining all the sensory faculties of perception to one of them, the noblest of which is sight. So sight dwells on a simple visible object until what he perceives and reports about it appears to him. It may be supposed that what these people see is on the surface of the mirror, but it is not so. Rather, they keep looking at the surface of the mirror until it vanishes from sight, and between them and the surface of the mirror there appears a veil like a cloud, in which forms take shape that are their perceptions; and they point out to them the thing intended, as to whatever they are turning to learn, whether denial or affirmation, and they report it in accordance with what they perceived. As for the mirror and the forms that can be perceived in it, they do not perceive them in that state; rather, by means of it this other kind of perception arises in them, which is of the soul, not a perception of sight, but one through which the object of the soul’s perception takes shape for the sense, as is well known. The same applies to those who look into the hearts and livers of animals, and into water and bowls and the like.

We have seen some of these who occupy the sense only with incense, then with incantations for predisposition, and then report what they perceived. They claim that they see forms embodied in the air that depict to them the circumstances of what they are turning to perceive, by likeness and sign. These people’s withdrawal from the senses is lighter than that of the former, and the world is a source of marvels. As for augury (zajr), it is what happens to some people of speaking about the unseen when a bird or an animal appears, and of reflecting on it after it has gone out of sight. It is a power in the soul that rouses eagerness and reflection about what is taken as an augury, whether seen or heard; the person’s imaginative faculty, as we said before, is strong, and he sets it to search, drawing on what he saw or heard, and that leads him to some perception, just as the imaginative faculty acts in sleep, when, at the stilling of the senses, it intervenes between what was sensed and seen in his waking state and combines it with what it has understood, and the dream vision results from it.

As for the insane, their rational souls are weakly attached to the body, because of the corruption of their temperaments for the most part and the weakness of the animal spirit in them. So the soul of such a person is neither absorbed in the senses nor immersed in them, because of what preoccupies it within itself, the pain of its deficiency and its sickness. Sometimes another spiritual being, a satanic one, competes with it for attachment to him and clings to him, and the soul is too weak to resist it, so that a seizure results. When that seizure strikes him, whether from the corruption of his temperament, arising from a corruption in the soul itself, or from the competition of satanic souls in their attachment to him, he is entirely absent from his sense, and perceives a flash from the world of his soul; some forms are imprinted in it and the imagination works them over. Sometimes speech issues from his tongue in that state, without his intending to speak. The perception of all of these is mixed, truth with falsehood, because they attain the connection, even though they lose sense, only after resorting to extraneous conceptions, as we have established; and from this falsehood enters these perceptions. As for the diviners, they are those who are attached to this perception but do not have that connection. So they set thought to work on the matter they are turning to, and proceed in it by conjecture and surmise, based on what they imagine to be the beginnings of that connection and perception, and they claim by this knowledge of the unseen, though in truth it is not of it. This is the sum of these matters. Al-Masʿūdī has spoken about them in the Murūj al-dhahab (“The Meadows of Gold”),

and he arrived at neither verification nor accuracy. It appears from the man’s words that he was far from being firmly grounded in the branches of knowledge, so that he reports what he heard from those qualified and those unqualified. All these perceptions that we have mentioned exist in the human species. The Arabs used to turn to the soothsayers to learn of events, and would bring their disputes to them, so that they might tell them the right in them from the perception of their unseen. There is much of that in the books of the people of literature. Famous among them in the pre-Islamic period were Shiqq ibn Anmār ibn Nizār and Saṭīḥ ibn Māzin ibn Ghassān. Saṭīḥ used to be rolled up as a garment is rolled up, and had no bone in him but the skull. Among the famous stories told about the two are the interpretation of the dream vision of Rabīʿa ibn Muḍar and what they told him of the kingship of the Abyssinians over Yemen and the kingship of Muḍar after them, and of the appearance of Muḥammadan prophecy among the Quraysh; and the dream vision of the Mūbadhān, which Saṭīḥ interpreted when Kisrā sent ʿAbd al-Masīḥ to him with it, and he told him of the matter of prophecy and the ruin of the kingship of Persia. All of this is well known. Likewise the diviners: there were many of them among the Arabs, and they mention them in their poetry. He said:
So I said to the diviner of al-Yamāma: cure me ... for if you cure me, you are truly a physician
And the other said:

I gave the diviner of al-Yamāma his judgment ... and the diviner of Najd, if only the two would cure me / and the two said, May God cure you! By God, we have no power ... over what your ribs carry of you

Among these perceptions of the unseen is what issues from some people, as they part from wakefulness and become mingled with sleep, of speech about the thing for which they long, giving what the unseen of that matter yields, as they wish. This occurs only at the beginning of sleep, as one parts from wakefulness and choice in speech has gone; he speaks as though compelled to speak, and the most he does is hear it and understand it. Likewise from those who are killed, when their heads and the middle parts of their bodies are severed, comes speech of that kind. It has reached us about some wicked tyrants that they killed persons from their prisons in order to learn from what they said at the killing the outcomes of their own affairs, and the victims told them what was hideous. Maslama mentioned in his Kitāb al-Ghāya, in a similar connection, that if a human being is put in a jar full of sesame oil and stays in it forty days, fed on figs and walnuts, until his flesh is gone and nothing is left of him but the veins and the sutures of his head, and he is then taken out of that oil, then, as soon as the air has dried upon him, he answers everything he is asked of the outcomes of matters, private and public. This is one of the abominable deeds of sorcerers, but from it the wonders of the human world can be understood. And among people [there are]

those who try to attain this perception of the unseen through spiritual exercise: by striving they attempt an artificial death, deadening all the bodily faculties, then effacing their traces with which the soul has been colored, then feeding it on invocation (dhikr) so that it grows stronger in its development; and this is achieved by concentration of thought and much hunger. It is known with certainty that when death descends on the body, sense and its veil go away and the soul is apprised of the hidden things. Among these are the people of magical spiritual exercise: they exercise themselves thus in order to gain knowledge of the hidden things and the ability to act in the worlds. Most of these are in the deviant zones, to the south and the north, especially the land of India, where they are called al-Ḥawkiyya (yogis); they have many books on how this spiritual exercise is carried out, and the reports about them in this are strange. As for the Sufis, their spiritual exercise is religious and bare of these blameworthy aims; they aim only at concentrating aspiration and turning wholly to God, so that the tastes of the people of gnosis and of divine unity may come to them. To concentration and hunger they add in their spiritual exercise nourishment by invocation, by which their orientation in this exercise is completed; for if the soul is brought up on invocation, it is closer to gnosis of God, and if it is bare of invocation, it is satanic. What comes to these Sufis of knowledge of the unseen and the ability to act is only incidental and is not intended from the outset, because if that is intended, the orientation in it is to other than God, being only for the purpose of acting and learning the unseen — and what a losing bargain it is! — for in truth it is polytheism (shirk). One of them said:

“Whoever prefers gnosis for the sake of gnosis has affirmed a second.” So by their orientation they aim at the One who is worshipped, for nothing other than Him. And if, in the course of it, something happens, it is incidental and not intended by them; many of them flee from it when it comes to them and pay no heed to it, wanting only God for His own sake and not for anything else. That this comes to them is well known. They call what comes to them of the unseen and of speech upon thoughts discernment (firāsa) and unveiling (kashf), and what comes to them of the ability to act saintly wonder. None of this is to be denied in their case. The master Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī and Abū Muḥammad ibn Abī Zayd al-Mālikī, with others, went so far as to deny it, to escape the confusion of the miracle (muʿjiza) with other things. But what the theologians rely on is that the distinction is achieved through the challenge (taḥaddī), and that is sufficient. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Among you there are those who are spoken to, and ʿUmar is one of them.” Well-known incidents of this kind occurred to the Companions that bear witness to this, such as the words of ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, “O Sāriya, the mountain!” This is Sāriya ibn Zunaym, who was commander of some of the Muslim armies in Iraq in the days of the conquests. He became entangled with the polytheists in a battle and was about to be routed, and he was near a mountain to which he could withdraw. That was made visible to ʿUmar while he was preaching from the pulpit in Medina, and he called out to him, “O Sāriya, the mountain!” and Sāriya heard him from where he stood, and saw his figure there. The story is well known. Something similar also happened to Abū Bakr in his bequest to his daughter ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with them both, concerning the wasqs of dates from his orchard that he had granted her; then he urged her to harvest them so that she might take possession of them apart from the heirs, and said in the course of his words, “They are only your two brothers and your two sisters.” She said, “There is only Asmāʾ; who is the other?” He said, “The one in the womb of Bint Khārija; I think it is a girl.” And it was a girl. This is recorded in the Muwaṭṭaʾ (“The Well-Trodden Path”), in the chapter on what is not permitted of gifts. Many such incidents occurred to them and to the righteous after them and to those who are taken as exemplars. Except that the Sufis say that it is rare in the time of prophecy, since in the presence of the prophet the novice has no state left, so much so that they say that when the novice comes to the city of the Prophet his state is taken from him as long as he is in it, until he leaves it. And may God grant us guidance and direct us to the truth.
